problem: Most object-goal navigation work uses discrete action policies (often RL) and frontier-only predictions, which do not exploit robot kinematics or provide dense representations suitable for planning and continuous control.
motivation: Real-world robots need continuous control and semantic context reasoning (e.g. couch near TV in living room). Dense cost maps are a natural interface for downstream planners like MPC, and mid-level visual features are known to help generalization.
key_idea: Predict dense, context-aware cost maps with a U-Net from partial semantic maps fused with orientation-binned mid-level visual representations, and drive the robot with a sampling-based IT-MPC in continuous velocity space.
insight: Mid-level representations (semantic seg., object classification, depth) add complementary cues: adding them to the semantic-map-only variant raises SR from 0.377 to 0.447 (7 points), and adding the semantic map to mid-level-only raises it 4.5 points. Pixel-level prediction metrics (mF1, mIOU) barely change or slightly drop, yet navigation improves, so navigation success is not tightly tied to those metrics. The gradient-direction loss is stated to yield smoother cost maps, though no ablation is shown.
method: Semantic mapping: following Chaplot et al., project GT Habitat semantic segmentation and depth into a top-down map with 16 semantic classes plus obstacle and explored masks; local (140x140) and global (420x420, avg-pooled) maps are concatenated.
Cost map network: U-Net with skip connections taking local+global semantic maps (36 channels), mid-level features, and a 64-d target category embedding tiled and concatenated at the latent level.

Oriented mid-level fusion: mid-level features (semantic segmentation, object classification, depth prediction from Sax et al.) from RGB are placed into one of 8 45° orientation bins matching the robot heading, with the rest zeroed, to align them with the map.

Multi-task decoders: one branch predicts occupancy (BCE), the other navigation cost (L1 over free cells plus a gradient-direction cosine loss); the occupancy mask thresholded and overlaid on the navigation cost. Weights are 1.0/1.5/1.0.
IT-MPC navigation: sampling-based information-theoretic MPC (horizon 50, noise sigma 0.35) scores sampled velocity sequences using the predicted cost map plus control effort.
Goal reacher: when the target appears in the local semantic map, an FMM cost map to the goal replaces the predicted cost; done is declared when cost <= 0.2.
Dataset: 48 filtered MP3D houses (36/4/8 train/val/test); GT cost maps from FMM; trajectories collected with a GT-cost IT-MPC agent, giving 171412/16209/41949 samples.

setting.backbone: U-Net cost map predictor (trained from scratch) + pre-trained mid-level encoders (Sax et al.) + IT-MPC
setting.training_data: Self-generated dataset from 36 MP3D training houses: 171k samples of semantic maps, RGB and GT FMM cost maps, collected by a GT-cost MPC agent
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth + GT semantic segmentation + odometry
setting.action_space: continuous velocity (linear and angular) of a differential drive robot
setting.privileged: GT semantic segmentation from the simulator and odometry; the random baseline is given the goal reacher; the upper-bound agent uses a GT cost map

numbers.eval_set_note: 8 held-out MP3D test houses, 40 random start positions each with random target from {bed, chair, sink, plant, couch}; 500 timesteps (50 s), success radius 1 m
numbers.backbone: U-Net cost map + mid-level features + IT-MPC

numbers_note: Values printed as fractions (e.g. 0.447) were converted to percent for SR and SPL. No standard benchmark is used; the evaluation is a custom MP3D setup. The GT cost map upper bound (SR 1.000, SPL 0.922) and privileged random baseline (SR 0.250, SPL 0.208) are baselines and are not listed.
results: The method reaches SR 0.447 and SPL 0.329 versus 0.250 / 0.208 for a privileged random agent, and produces smoother trajectories with lower acceleration and jerk. It is far from the GT-cost-map upper bound (SR 1.0). Fusing mid-level representations improves SR by 7 points over the semantic-map-only variant.
limitations: Uses GT simulator semantic segmentation and only simulated MP3D; no real-robot experiments, and noise and uncertainty are not handled.
Only weak baselines (privileged random and GT upper bound); no comparison to other semantic navigation methods, and the evaluation is small and custom (320 episodes, 5 categories).
Preliminary results with low absolute success (44.7%) and low aAP scores; the gradient loss is not ablated.
